blocks.content: Two rounds that both involve code and design but they test completely different things. Walking into one expecting the other is one of the fastest ways to fail.
1. What each round actually is
LLD tests your design thinking, while Machine Coding tests your ability to convert that design into clean, working code under time constraints.
blocks.text: LLD tests your design thinking, while Machine Coding tests your ability to convert that design into clean, working code under time constraints.

blocks.content: LLD ROUND
You are given a real-world system to design "design a parking lot", "design a split wise clone". You think out loud, sketch classes, define relationships, and apply design patterns.
You may write some code, but the focus is on structure and thought process not working output.
MACHINE CODING ROUND
You are given a problem and asked to write working, runnable code usually in 60 to 90 minutes. The code must compile, handle edge cases, and produce correct output.
Design matters, but the primary bar is: does it actually work?
THE CORE DIFFERENCE

blocks.content: 3. Same problem, different expectations
Take "design an ATM machine." Here's how each round approaches it differently.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512552064-492595731.png
blocks.alt: Diagram showing what each round evaluates for the same ATM design prompt, reasoning and tradeoffs in the LLD round versus running code in the Machine Coding round

blocks.content: IN AN LLD ROUND
You identify classes: ATM, Card, Account, Transaction, CashDispenser.
You apply the State pattern for ATM states: Idle → CardInserted → PinVerified → Dispensing.
You define interfaces like AuthenticationServiceand explain why it's an interface and not a concrete class.
Interviewer asks trade-offs. You discuss. Code may never be written at all.
IN A MACHINE CODING ROUND
You write the classes, wire them together, and handle the full user flow: insert card → enter PIN → choose amount → dispense cash → print receipt.
Edge cases must work: wrong PIN 3 times locks the account. Insufficient funds shows an error. Balance updates persist across transactions.
At the end, the interviewer runs your code.
4. How to prepare for each
LLD PREP

["Study OOP pillars and SOLID principles deeply not just definitions, but when to apply each.
","Learn the 5 to 6 most common design patterns: Singleton, Factory, Strategy, Observer, Decorator, State.
","Practice drawing class diagrams for real systems. Parking lot, library, chess, hotel booking, food delivery.
","Practice talking through your design out loud. Interviewers grade your reasoning, not just your output.
"]
items: Study OOP pillars and SOLID principles deeply not just definitions, but when to apply each.
Learn the 5 to 6 most common design patterns: Singleton, Factory, Strategy, Observer, Decorator, State.
Practice drawing class diagrams for real systems. Parking lot, library, chess, hotel booking, food delivery.
Practice talking through your design out loud. Interviewers grade your reasoning, not just your output.

blocks.content: MACHINE CODING PREP

["Practice building complete, working mini-systems in 60 to 90 minutes. Use a real IDE, set a timer.
","Focus on clean code habits meaningful names, small methods, no god classes under time pressure.
","Master your language's standard library cold. Sorting, collections, string handling these shouldn't slow you down.
","Always handle edge cases before submitting: nulls, empty inputs, boundary conditions.
"]
items: Practice building complete, working mini-systems in 60 to 90 minutes. Use a real IDE, set a timer.
Focus on clean code habits meaningful names, small methods, no god classes under time pressure.
Master your language's standard library cold. Sorting, collections, string handling these shouldn't slow you down.
Always handle edge cases before submitting: nulls, empty inputs, boundary conditions.

blocks.content: THE TRAP MOST PEOPLE FALL INTO: Spending all prep time on LLD design theory and walking into a machine coding round unable to write clean, working code fast or the reverse: grinding implementation problems and being unable to articulate design decisions out loud. Both rounds need specific, separate practice.

THE OVERLAP: Clean class design helps you in both. A well-structured LLD makes the machine coding round faster. And writing real code in machine coding rounds deepens your LLD instincts. They reinforce each other do both.
5. Common formats companies use

Neither round looks the same everywhere. The label on the calendar invite might say "LLD interview" or "machine coding round," but the actual format, tooling, and time pressure vary a lot company to company. Knowing the format ahead of time changes how you should prepare.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512554640-817611570.png
blocks.alt: Diagram showing how an interview invite branches into LLD round formats and Machine Coding round formats

blocks.content: LLD ROUND FORMATS
Most LLD rounds fall into one of a few shapes, and the shape decides how much you should lean on talking versus writing.

["Verbal only, no artifacts: you talk through the design and the interviewer takes notes, nothing gets written down by you at all.","Shared virtual whiteboard such as Excalidraw or Miro where you sketch boxes and arrows for classes and relationships as you talk.","A plain document or text editor where you type class names, method signatures, and short comments, but nothing needs to compile.","Panel format with two interviewers in the room, one driving the questions and one silently scoring how you reason."]
items: Verbal only, no artifacts: you talk through the design and the interviewer takes notes, nothing gets written down by you at all.
Shared virtual whiteboard such as Excalidraw or Miro where you sketch boxes and arrows for classes and relationships as you talk.
A plain document or text editor where you type class names, method signatures, and short comments, but nothing needs to compile.
Panel format with two interviewers in the room, one driving the questions and one silently scoring how you reason.

blocks.content: MACHINE CODING ROUND FORMATS
Machine coding rounds are more standardized because the whole point is producing something that runs, but the delivery mechanism still differs.

["Standalone timed round on a platform such as CoderPad or HackerRank, with a visible countdown and an execution button.","Take home assignment with a git repository to submit, reviewed asynchronously by the team over the following days.","Pair programming style where the interviewer watches you code live on a shared screen and occasionally asks questions.","Onsite room with just an IDE and no internet access, closer to how you would actually work day to day on the job."]
items: Standalone timed round on a platform such as CoderPad or HackerRank, with a visible countdown and an execution button.
Take home assignment with a git repository to submit, reviewed asynchronously by the team over the following days.
Pair programming style where the interviewer watches you code live on a shared screen and occasionally asks questions.
Onsite room with just an IDE and no internet access, closer to how you would actually work day to day on the job.

blocks.content: 6. Worked example, parking lot as an LLD discussion
blocks.text: 6. Worked example, parking lot as an LLD discussion

blocks.content: Take the classic prompt, design a parking lot system. Here is how the exact same problem plays out completely differently depending on which round you are sitting in.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512556231-452181204.png
blocks.alt: Diagram of the parking lot LLD discussion flow from naming entities to justifying patterns to sketching signatures

blocks.content: HOW THE CONVERSATION UNFOLDS
In an LLD round you start by naming the entities out loud: ParkingLot, Level, Slot, Vehicle, Ticket, Payment. You explain how they relate to each other before writing anything.

Then you justify your patterns. A single shared ParkingLot instance suggests Singleton. Different fee rules for cars, bikes, and trucks suggest Strategy. Creating the right Vehicle subtype from a plate or ticket suggests Factory. The interviewer cares less about the pattern names and more about why each one earns its place.
WHAT YOU SKETCH, NOT WHAT YOU SHIP
blocks.text: WHAT YOU SKETCH, NOT WHAT YOU SHIP

blocks.content: On a whiteboard or shared document you would sketch something like this, method signatures only, bodies left as comments. Nobody expects this to compile.
WHAT THE INTERVIEWER IS GRADING

["Whether you identified the right entities and relationships without being told them.","Whether you can justify why a pattern fits, not just name drop it because it sounds impressive.","How you handle a curveball, such as adding monthly passes or electric vehicle charging slots mid-conversation.","Whether your design would still make sense if the lot had ten levels instead of one."]
items: Whether you identified the right entities and relationships without being told them.
Whether you can justify why a pattern fits, not just name drop it because it sounds impressive.
How you handle a curveball, such as adding monthly passes or electric vehicle charging slots mid-conversation.
Whether your design would still make sense if the lot had ten levels instead of one.

blocks.content: 7. Worked example, parking lot as a machine coding submission
blocks.text: 7. Worked example, parking lot as a machine coding submission

blocks.content: Same prompt, completely different bar. Now you are told: design and build a working parking lot system in 75 minutes that supports parking a vehicle, unparking it, and printing a receipt with the fee due.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512557919-589087511.png
blocks.alt: Diagram of the parking lot machine coding flow from parking a vehicle to computing the fee and printing a receipt

blocks.content: WHAT MUST ACTUALLY RUN

["Assign the nearest available slot to an incoming vehicle, and reject entry cleanly when the lot is full.","Track the entry time per ticket so the fee can be computed from the actual duration parked.","Free the slot on unparking and make it available again immediately for the next vehicle.","Return a receipt showing the ticket id, duration, and amount due, with numbers that are actually correct."]
items: Assign the nearest available slot to an incoming vehicle, and reject entry cleanly when the lot is full.
Track the entry time per ticket so the fee can be computed from the actual duration parked.
Free the slot on unparking and make it available again immediately for the next vehicle.
Return a receipt showing the ticket id, duration, and amount due, with numbers that are actually correct.

blocks.content: There is no time budget for five design patterns here. A plain class with a map and a queue that works beats an elaborate hierarchy that does not compile.

codes.python:
import time


class Ticket:
    def __init__(self, ticket_id, vehicle_number, slot_id, entry_time):
        self.ticket_id = ticket_id
        self.vehicle_number = vehicle_number
        self.slot_id = slot_id
        self.entry_time = entry_time


class ParkingLot:
    def __init__(self, total_slots, rate_per_hour):
        self.rate_per_hour = rate_per_hour
        self.free_slots = list(range(1, total_slots + 1))
        self.tickets = {}
        self.next_ticket_id = 1

    def park(self, vehicle_number):
        if not self.free_slots:
            raise Exception("Parking lot is full")
        slot_id = self.free_slots.pop(0)
        ticket = Ticket(self.next_ticket_id, vehicle_number, slot_id, time.time())
        self.tickets[ticket.ticket_id] = ticket
        self.next_ticket_id += 1
        return ticket

    def unpark(self, ticket_id, exit_time=None):
        if ticket_id not in self.tickets:
            raise Exception("Invalid ticket")
        ticket = self.tickets.pop(ticket_id)
        exit_time = exit_time if exit_time is not None else time.time()
        hours = max(1, int((exit_time - ticket.entry_time) // 3600) + 1)
        fee = hours * self.rate_per_hour
        self.free_slots.append(ticket.slot_id)
        return {"ticket_id": ticket_id, "hours": hours, "fee": fee}


lot = ParkingLot(2, 20)
t1 = lot.park("KA-01-HH-1234")
lot.park("KA-02-MM-5678")
print("Issued ticket", t1.ticket_id, "for slot", t1.slot_id)
print("Receipt:", lot.unpark(t1.ticket_id, t1.entry_time + 2 * 3600))

blocks.content: WHAT THE INTERVIEWER IS GRADING
Correctness on edge cases like a full lot or an invalid ticket, whether it compiles and runs without hand holding, and whether you managed the clock well enough to actually finish and demo it.

blocks.title: Same design, two different bars
blocks.text: The LLD round rewards the class diagram itself and the reasoning behind choosing Strategy for pricing and Singleton for the lot instance. The machine coding round does not care about any of that reasoning if park and unpark do not actually work end to end inside the timer, with the fee coming out correct.

blocks.content: 8. Training the specific skill each round demands
blocks.text: 8. Training the specific skill each round demands

blocks.content: Section 4 covered what to study for each round. This section covers the practice habits that actually build the skill, since reading about a topic and being able to perform it live under pressure are not the same thing.
BUILDING LLD VERBAL FLUENCY

Record yourself explaining a design out loud for five minutes without touching a keyboard. Listen back for the moments you go quiet or trail off, those are the spots that will hurt you in a real round.
Practice on a physical whiteboard or plain paper so drawing a class diagram becomes fast and automatic, not something you are figuring out for the first time in front of an interviewer.
Do mock interviews where the only rule is that you narrate every decision and every trade-off as you make it, even the ones that feel obvious.
BUILDING MACHINE CODING SPEED
Run drills with a visible timer on small, complete programs, not partial snippets. The goal is finishing something end to end, not writing a lot of code.
Memorize your language collection APIs cold: sorting, maps, queues, string handling. Every second spent searching documentation mid-round is a second you do not get back.
Practice typing out full class hierarchies rather than pseudocode, and force yourself to finish a small runnable program from scratch every day for a couple of weeks before a machine coding round.

blocks.title: Practice under the conditions of the actual round
blocks.content: Reading about design patterns will not make you fast on a whiteboard, and reading about clean code will not make you fast at the keyboard. Rehearse the exact activity: verbal explanation and diagramming for one round, timed typing and complete implementations for the other. The two skills do not transfer to each other automatically.
9. Common mistakes in each round
The same instinct that helps you in one round can actively hurt you in the other. Here is where candidates most often trip up.

{"headers":["Mistake","In an LLD round","In a machine coding round"],"rows":[["Over-engineering","Adding five design patterns to a system that only needed one, just to show you know them","Building an elaborate class hierarchy instead of a small working solution, then running out of time"],["Under-communicating","Designing silently in your head and only revealing the final answer at the end","Going quiet for forty minutes and only showing code right before time runs out"],["Ignoring constraints","Skipping stated requirements like concurrency or scale because the diagram looks cleaner without them","Skipping stated edge cases like empty input or duplicate entries because handling them takes extra time"],["Wrong depth for the round","Jumping straight to code instead of first agreeing on entities and responsibilities","Spending the first thirty minutes debating design patterns instead of writing code"]]}

Notice the pattern: almost every mistake in one column is the same instinct applied in the wrong round. The fix is not learning more theory, it is learning to recognize which round you are in and switching modes deliberately.
10. Figuring out which round you are walking into
blocks.text: 10. Figuring out which round you are walking into

blocks.content: Job descriptions and interview process emails rarely spell this out plainly. It is worth just asking rather than guessing and preparing for the wrong thing.

["Ask the recruiter directly whether you are expected to submit compiling code or just discuss a design verbally.","Ask whether the round is timed strictly or open ended with back and forth discussion built in.","Ask what tool you will use: a shared document, a whiteboard app, or an actual IDE with a run button.","Read the process email for verbs. Words like implement and submit usually signal machine coding. Words like design and discuss usually signal LLD."]
items: Ask the recruiter directly whether you are expected to submit compiling code or just discuss a design verbally.
Ask whether the round is timed strictly or open ended with back and forth discussion built in.
Ask what tool you will use: a shared document, a whiteboard app, or an actual IDE with a run button.
Read the process email for verbs. Words like implement and submit usually signal machine coding. Words like design and discuss usually signal LLD.

blocks.content: If the recruiter cannot answer, treat it as a signal to prepare for both in miniature rather than betting everything on one format.
11. The bottom line
Both rounds are trying to answer the same underlying question, can this person build maintainable software, they are just asking it in different formats and under different constraints.

An LLD round wants to see how you think before a single line of code is committed. A machine coding round wants to see whether that thinking survives contact with a compiler and a clock. Strong engineers train for both separately, because the overlap between them is real but it is not automatic.
Walk into each round knowing exactly which one it is, prepare the specific skill it demands, and you remove most of the surprise before you even sit down.
12. A quick self-check before you walk in
blocks.text: 12. A quick self-check before you walk in

blocks.content: A few minutes before the round starts, or the night before, run through these questions so you switch into the right mode instead of defaulting to whichever one feels more comfortable.

["Do I know whether I need to produce working code, or just a design and a conversation?","If code is expected, have I practiced typing a complete small program under a real timer this week?","If no code is expected, have I practiced explaining a design out loud without writing anything down?","Do I know the two or three design patterns most likely to fit whatever prompt shows up, and can I justify each one in a sentence?"]
items: Do I know whether I need to produce working code, or just a design and a conversation?
If code is expected, have I practiced typing a complete small program under a real timer this week?
If no code is expected, have I practiced explaining a design out loud without writing anything down?
Do I know the two or three design patterns most likely to fit whatever prompt shows up, and can I justify each one in a sentence?

blocks.content: If you can answer all four without hesitating, you are prepared for the format, not just the topic, and that is the distinction that actually matters in the room.
None of this replaces knowing the fundamentals. It just makes sure the fundamentals you already have get expressed in the way the specific round is actually measuring.
